extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of history; teachers and writers of popular history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and editing history for a general readership, covering choices of spelling/transliteration, citation practice, handling controversial claims, use of archaeological evidence, and pedagogical bibliographic recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use time-established spelling for historical names
rubrics_metrics.description: “It will probably save school teachers of history from endless confusion and muddle if they adhere firmly to the time-established spelling.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the conventional English forms (e.g., Jehovah, Confucius) rather than newly proposed phonetic spellings; established spellings help general readers follow narratives and prevent confusion across different accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'dazzle-spelling' and excessive phonetic exactitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern writers in their zeal for phonetics seem to have lost their sense of proportion. This treatment of old forms has much the same effect as the dazzle-painting of ships ... It is dazzle-spelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt variable or hyper‑phonetic spellings (T'sin, Sin, Chin, T'chin mixed together). Prioritize clarity and the reader's ability to recognize names over narrow phonetic accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe limits to pedantic classicalism
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nevertheless, there are limits to this classicism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some classical spellings may be defensible, avoid pedantry that makes texts less accessible; strike a balance between scholarly forms and established English usage (examples: Peisistratus used over Pisistratus in this work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about variant name spellings and inform the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: There are variants to these names, and to most Egyptian names, for few self-respecting Egyptologists will tolerate the spelling of their colleagues. ... It is desirable that the reader should know such variations exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When names have multiple acceptable spellings, note variants so readers recognize the same person/place in other sources; explain chosen conventions in an editorial note if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer readability (Europeanized forms) for the general reader
rubrics_metrics.description: “A boldly Europeanized name, such as Confucius, is far more readily grasped.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For popular and teaching texts, choose forms that are familiar and easy to read rather than obscure transliterations that impede comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge differing authorities and date uncertainties
rubrics_metrics.description: “Authorities vary upon this date. Some put back Sargon I to 3750 B.C. This latter was his traditional date based on Babylonian records.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dates or facts are contested among scholars, indicate the range of opinions and cite the relevant authorities rather than presenting a single dogmatic date as absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag controversial matters and direct readers to current debates
rubrics_metrics.description: “Here we touch on highly controversial matters. The reader interested in the question ... should consult Nature, Jan. 27, 1916, Spinden and Elliot Smith in discussion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly mark topics that are contested and provide references to the scholarly literature or debates so interested readers can follow up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support assertions with citations to primary and authoritative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous footnotes and ‘See …’ references (e.g., to excavations, to Sir H. H. Johnston, to Breasted) are used throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Back up historical claims with references to excavations, primary texts, and reputable secondary literature; use citations liberally for claims that depend on specialist evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on primary archaeological reports and fieldwork for archaeological claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Excavations conducted at Eridu by Capt. R. Campbell Thompson during the recent war have revealed an early Neolithic agricultural stage ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making archaeological or material-culture claims, base statements on published excavations and reports; cite the relevant field investigators and publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dogmatism; present alternative interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: “This is, I think, too dogmatic about Helen. ... It looks to me as if there was some strong motive for building just there, and an equally strong motive for great confederacies destroying the city when built.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer multiple plausible explanations for historical phenomena where evidence admits more than one reading; state the author’s view but acknowledge other scholars’ positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use well-known chronological anchors for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: “776 B.C. is the year of the First Olympiad, a valuable starting-point in Greek chronology.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor narratives to widely recognized chronological markers (Olympiads, regnal years, widely accepted BCE/CE dates) to help readers situate events in time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider linguistic structure when interpreting thought and literature
rubrics_metrics.description: On Chinese: the Chinaman gives the bare cores of his meaning; the Englishman gets to it by a bold metaphor. ... Chinese thought is kept practical and restricted by the limitations upon metaphor the linguistic structure of Chinese imposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing literary or intellectual history, take into account how the grammar and structure of languages shape modes of thought and expression; use linguistic analysis to explain differences in metaphor, imagery, and conceptualisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide recommended readings and accessible secondary works for students
rubrics_metrics.description: The student who finds this subject of philological history interesting, should read the introduction to the same writer’s Comparative Study ... A very handy book for the student in this section is Abbott’s Skeleton Outline of Greek History.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include short bibliographic recommendations (handbooks, introductions, readable syntheses) aimed at students or general readers to guide further study.
